extracted.intended_audience: creative writers (authors, novelists, fanfiction/adaptation writers) interested in using public-domain characters and settings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for using public-domain works, characters, and settings in original fiction — including how to verify what is actually public domain, what to avoid (elements added by later adaptations), and how to leverage the public-domain material creatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use only material from the original work, not later media creations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure what you are using is part of the original work, and not something created by Disney or another movie company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: the crocodile's name 'Tick-Tock' and many songs are not in Barrie's original Peter Pan; the ruby slippers are a film invention (the original book had silver shoes). Anti-pattern: assuming iconic movie elements are public domain. Practical rule: verify that a character detail, name, prop, or song appears in the original text/issue before using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify works' public-domain status by publication date (the '96 years' rule referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything before 96 years from now is public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers repeatedly cite 'anything older than 96 years' as entering the public domain; they also note gray areas and emphasise doing your research. Note that works enter at the start of the calendar year and lists can be misleading; confirm dates with reliable sources rather than a single quick search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research specific elements because estates/adaptors can claim later-added elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some elements from later stories or adaptations may not be public domain even if earlier stories are — estates or rights-holders have litigated to assert rights over particular elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sherlock Holmes — early stories are public domain but the estate has successfully argued that certain later-introduced elements (e.g., particular portrayals of the Holmes–Watson relationship) remain protected. Guidance: research case law and rights assertions for high-profile properties; avoid relying on assumptions about character relationships or portrayals that originated later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that works enter the public domain incrementally (year-by-year/issue-by-issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements from specific early publications enter public domain first; later additions in subsequent issues/years may remain protected until their own term expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Superman's early appearances (where he couldn't fly) enter separately from later issues that introduced iconic villains or powers. Practical implication: only use elements that actually appear in the specific works that are in the public domain; don't assume the whole franchise is free at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t rely on a single quick online list — confirm with multiple sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick Google lists can be useful but may be inaccurate or misread lead times; verify before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers noted Googling 'entering the public domain in 2022' and warned listeners to get a second source. Anti-pattern: writing and publishing based on a single, unchecked list and then discovering you were a year early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retelling and expanding on public-domain works is permitted and valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: Retelling is fine! You can use public-domain characters and settings to tell new stories, including radical reimaginings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative opportunities include retellings, genre shifts (e.g., cyberpunk Peter Pan), and bringing minor or epigraph characters into prominence. This allows you to leverage an established universe without needing permission or licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public-domain material to leverage shared narrative knowledge and create effective twists
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing builds on shared understanding; twists play off audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because readers share cultural touchstones, you can craft efficient pitches and surprising twists by subverting expectations tied to well-known public-domain material (example: 'this, but 20 years later and with this twist'). This is a creative strategy rather than a legal rule, but it's an explicit recommendation of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of legislative or industry actions that can affect public-domain timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and lobbying (e.g., copyright-term extensions like the Sonny Bono Act) can change when works enter the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers warned that rights-holders (e.g., Disney) might push to extend terms in the future, which could delay when certain characters/franchises enter the public domain. Practical takeaway: stay informed of legislative developments affecting copyright terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical exercise: find something entering the public domain and write a story about it
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: Find something entering the public domain, and write a story about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit call to action to practice using public-domain material. Use it to apply the other rubrics: verify the element's origin, confirm public-domain status, and then retell or expand creatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage lesser-known aspects and minor characters from original works
rubrics_metrics.description: You get to use an established universe, and you can bring out lesser-known aspects and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an epigraph or small aside in the original can become the seed of a major character or plotline in your new work. This is presented as a creative advantage of writing in the public domain.
